text: This is the first real quantum error-correcting code in the course — small enough to trace by hand completely, and the direct ancestor of every stabilizer code that follows.

The 3-qubit bit-flip code encodes a logical qubit as ket-zero-L equals ket-triple-zero, ket-one-L equals ket-triple-one. Given an unknown data qubit alpha ket-zero plus beta ket-one and two ancillas starting in ket-zero, the encoding circuit is just two CNOT gates: qubit 1 onto qubit 2, then qubit 1 onto qubit 3. Each CNOT entangles rather than clones, and the joint state becomes alpha ket-triple-zero plus beta ket-triple-one — a genuinely entangled 3-qubit state. No single qubit, taken alone, holds alpha and beta.

The protection comes from two stabilizer measurements: Z1Z2, comparing qubits 1 and 2, and Z2Z3, comparing qubits 2 and 3. Both the all-zeros and all-ones logical states are plus-1 eigenstates of both operators, so measuring either one on an error-free encoded state always returns plus-1, no disagreement, without revealing alpha or beta at all.

Injecting a single X error at each of the 3 qubit positions and measuring both stabilizers gives this verified table, starting from logical zero: no error gives syndrome 00, no correction needed. An error on qubit 1 gives syndrome 10, correct by flipping qubit 1. Qubit 2 gives syndrome 11, flip qubit 2. Qubit 3 gives syndrome 01, flip qubit 3. Every one of these four cases decodes correctly, 100% of the time — the two-bit syndrome alone identifies exactly which qubit was hit, without ever needing to know alpha or beta.

But this code provides zero protection against a phase-flip error. A Z error on any of the 3 qubits changes the relative phase of the superposition without flipping any computational-basis bit value, so it produces no disagreement in either stabilizer — the syndrome reads 00, as if nothing happened, while the logical state has actually been corrupted.
Protecting against phase errors needs a different, complementary code — built next: the three-qubit phase-flip code, the exact mirror image of what you just saw.
